activities.anchor: 80% of the work and 100% of the reputation risk
activities.caption: call the share of the work that is cleaning
activities.name: cleanShareEst

config.prompt: By practitioner consensus, roughly what share of a data project's work is cleaning?
config.why: About 80% — which is why the discipline of profiling, deciding, encoding and validating is the profession's core skill, not a chore before the real work.
config.context: the glamorous 20% assumes the 80% was done honestly

activities.anchor: Knowing the sources tells you where to look
activities.caption: pair each source with its characteristic failures
activities.name: cleanSourceMatch

config.prompt: Pair each data source with the mess it characteristically produces:

pairs.right: transpositions (31 typed as 13) and free-text vocabularies
gaps when offline, spikes at interference, slow drift
identity problems — 'J Smith' and 'Smith, John' — and schema disagreements
encoding rot ('café' to 'cafÃ©') and silent truncation

config.why: Messy data is archaeology: each oddity is a fossil of how the data was captured, merged or typed — so the first question is never 'what is wrong?' but 'where did this come from?'

activities.anchor: Ten minutes of profiling just produced
activities.caption: rebuild the order of operations
activities.name: cleanProfileOrder

config.prompt: Rebuild the cleaning order of operations:
items: Profile — count missing, distinct, min/max, sample the weird rows
Hypothesise — what mechanism produced each anomaly?
Fix — apply the treatment the mechanism justifies
Document — record every decision so the step can rerun
config.why: Profile first, hypothesise second, fix third, document always — fixing before profiling means fixing your guesses.

activities.anchor: Two rows with the same customer ID are not duplicates
activities.caption: bet before you read on — the duplicate verdict
activities.name: cleanDupePredict

config.q: Your table shows two rows with the same customer ID. Are they duplicates?
choices: Not necessarily — if each row is an order, the customer key repeating is correct; the unit of analysis defines the key
Yes — the same ID appearing twice is always a duplicate
Only if the email addresses also match
config.why: 'Duplicate' is meaningless until you define what makes two rows the same thing — one row per order, per customer, or per customer-month gives three different answers.

activities.anchor: Missing data is not one problem but three
activities.caption: file each gap under its missingness mechanism
activities.name: cleanMechSort

config.prompt: File each case of missing data under its mechanism:

items.label: younger users skip the phone field — but you know their age
the highest earners skip the income question
the sickest patients skip the follow-up visit

config.why: Only missing-completely-at-random is safe to drop; when missingness relates to the unobserved value itself, dropping biases every statistic silently.

activities.caption: the delete key or the root-cause question
activities.name: cleanOutlierBranch

config.root: Your sales table contains one transaction of 4,999,999 — far beyond every other row.

choices.label: Delete it — no single sale is that big
choices.feedback: It may be the whale customer — the most important row in the dataset, deleted on reflex.

choices.label: Investigate before touching: impossible or implausible?
choices.feedback: The distinction that matters: impossible values are errors to fix; implausible values are findings to investigate.

choices.label: Replace it with the average transaction value
choices.feedback: Imputing over a finding manufactures agreement where the world had variation.

whale.text: Revenue charts now look tidy — and the customer who paid 4,999,999 is gone from every average.

choices.label: Restore it and ask why the column contains it
choices.feedback: A root-cause question ('why does this column contain this?') instead of a delete key.

rootcause.text: The diagnosis decides the treatment: a bug gets fixed, a whale gets studied.

impute.text: The average now includes a value nobody observed — the dataset lies more quietly than before.

config.why: An age of 250 is a bug; a transaction of 4,999,999 may be the finding you most need to understand — investigate implausible values before touching them.

activities.anchor: The retraction-grade errors are usually unglamorous
activities.caption: find the backwards habit — types, encodings, timezones
activities.name: cleanTypesSpot

config.prompt: One of these data-hygiene habits is backwards — click it:
lines: ZIP codes stored as numbers lose their leading zeros.
IDs stored as floats are silently rounded past 15 digits.
UTF-8 read as Latin-1 garbles every accented character.
Keep timestamps in whatever local timezone each source system used.
config.correction: Parse dates explicitly with a stated timezone and keep one canonical timezone internally — mixing local times shifts daily aggregates and duplicates or deletes an hour at every daylight-saving boundary.
config.why: The defences are habits, not cleverness: parse explicitly, canonicalise, store types in a schema — not in hope.

activities.anchor: Clean is not a state, it is a property
activities.caption: true or false — the permanence of clean
activities.name: cleanValidJudge

config.statement: A dataset that was cleaned and validated last month is still clean today.
config.why: False — data rots upstream: schemas drift, partners change exports, a 'temporary' fix ships on a Friday. That is why professional cleaning is assertions that re-run on every load, so something screams instead of a dashboard quietly turning wrong.

activities.caption: file each profiled anomaly under its treatment
activities.name: cleanWorkedSort

config.prompt: From the worked session — file each anomaly under the treatment it was given:

items.label: prices stored as text with thousands separators
dates before 2000 or after next year

config.why: Negatives are real transactions net revenue needs; parseable text gets a rule; junk dates are counted, because counting junk is monitoring.
